corpus_definition: A group of animals that might soon die out forever.
usage_note: Countable noun phrase: 'an endangered species', 'endangered species' (the plural is the same). Often with 'protect' or 'save': 'protect endangered species'. Can also be used for plants.

relations.note: Very close; used by scientists for animals and plants that are in danger but often a little less at risk.
Wildlife means all wild animals and plants, not only the ones in danger.
An extinct animal has already died out; an endangered species may still be saved.

context.text: The snow leopard is an endangered species, and a few still live in the mountains of Uzbekistan. Rangers work hard to protect endangered species from hunters.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; plural has the same form. 'Extinct' given as related, not antonym.

corpus_definition: To make sure that people follow the laws and rules.

forms.definition: the act of making people obey laws or rules
forms.example: Stricter enforcement of speed limits has made the roads safer.

syn.note: Related: putting a rule into use; enforcement is stronger and often involves the police.
Related and formal: putting a plan or law into action.

forms.definition: to make sure that people obey a law or rule
forms.example: The police are here to enforce the new traffic laws.

syn.note: Impose means to introduce a rule and force people to accept it.
Easier word: to use a rule in a situation; enforce adds the idea of punishment if people do not obey.
Easy phrasal verb: to do what a law or plan says.

ant.note: When officials ignore a rule, they do nothing to make people obey it.

forms.definition: able to be made legal and obeyed, for example by a court
forms.example: This contract is not legally enforceable.

syn.note: A binding agreement must be obeyed by law.
Valid means legally accepted; it is a little wider in meaning.

ant.note: A rule that is impossible to make people obey.

forms.note: No common adverb exists in this family.

people.definition: a person whose job is to make others obey rules
people.example: The new manager acted as the enforcer of company rules.

context.text: The city of Tashkent decided to enforce the no-smoking rule in parks. Police say enforcement will start next month, and people who break the rule will pay a fine.

reviewer_note: No en- affix claimed: enforce is not clearly en- + force for learners. 'Law enforcement' is the most common collocation.

corpus_definition: To make something better or improve its value.

forms.definition: an improvement that makes something better, stronger or more valuable
forms.example: The new software includes several security enhancements.

syn.note: Very close and more common in everyday English.
Often used for computers, phones and machines.
An increase that helps something; a little informal.

ant.note: The process of becoming worse.

forms.definition: to make something better, stronger or more attractive
forms.example: These herbs will enhance the flavor of the soup.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with almost the same meaning.
Boost means to increase or make stronger; a little informal.
Increase is about size or amount; enhance is about quality.
Easy phrase: 'The music added to the atmosphere.'

ant.note: To make something worse or less attractive.
To make something smaller or less.

forms.definition: made better, stronger or more advanced than before
forms.example: The phone has an enhanced camera with better night photos.

syn.note: Easier word with the same meaning.
Very easy, general word.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Aziza added fresh herbs to enhance the taste of her plov. Her brother said it was a real enhancement to the old family recipe.

reviewer_note: Enhancer (thing, as in flavour enhancer) left out: not a learner-dictionary headword in Oxford/Cambridge.

corpus_definition: a feeling of great excitement and interest about something

forms.definition: a strong feeling of excitement and interest in something
forms.example: She shows great enthusiasm for her new project.

syn.note: Eagerness is a strong wish to do something soon.
Easy word; excitement can be short, enthusiasm usually lasts longer.
Passion is an even stronger feeling of love for an activity.
Easy word, but weaker: you can be interested without being excited.

ant.note: Not caring about something at all.
Formal: having no interest or energy to do anything.

forms.definition: to talk about something in a very excited way
forms.example: He enthused about his trip to Khiva for an hour.

syn.note: Informal: to talk about something you like very much.
To say good things about something, but calmly.

forms.definition: feeling or showing a lot of excitement and interest
forms.example: The students were very enthusiastic about the trip.

syn.note: Wanting very much to do something.
Common in British English: 'keen on football'.
Easy word; excited is often about a coming event.
Stronger: you love the activity deeply.

ant.note: Showing no excitement or interest.
Not caring at all.

forms.definition: in a very excited and interested way
forms.example: The crowd cheered enthusiastically when the team scored.

syn.note: With a strong wish to do something.
Easy word for showing excitement.
With great interest.

ant.note: Without much interest or effort.

people.definition: a person who is very interested in a hobby or activity
people.example: My uncle is a car enthusiast and reads every car magazine.

context.text: Our new teacher has so much enthusiasm for English. The class is enthusiastic too, and everyone answers enthusiastically when she asks a question.

reviewer_note: Unenthusiastic is placed as antonym, not a form. Enthuse is a back-formation from enthusiasm, still the same family.

corpus_definition: Feeling very happy and interested in doing something.
usage_note: be/feel/seem enthusiastic about + noun or -ing: 'She is enthusiastic about learning Korean.' Also 'very enthusiastic about'.

relations.note: Very close, common in British English: 'keen on sport'.
Easy phrase; often about something that will happen soon.
Easy, but weaker: interest without much excitement.
Not caring about something at all.

context.text: The students are enthusiastic about the science trip to the Tashkent planetarium. Even Bekzod, who is usually quiet, seems enthusiastic about going.

reviewer_note: Adjective + preposition pattern; followed by noun or -ing.

corpus_definition: the state where everyone has the same rights and opportunities

forms.definition: the situation in which all people have the same rights and chances
forms.example: We must fight for equality for all people.

syn.note: Easy word: treating people in a right and honest way.
Fair treatment by the law and society; a wider idea.
Formal: being at the same level, often about pay.

ant.note: When some people have more rights, money or chances than others.
Treating some people worse because of who they are.

forms.definition: to make things the same in size, amount or level
forms.example: The new law aims to equalize pay for men and women.
forms.note: British spelling: equalise. In football it also means to score a goal that makes the score level.

syn.note: Easy phrasal verb: make differences smaller.
To make two sides the same in weight or importance.

forms.definition: the same in size, number, value or rights
forms.example: All citizens should have equal rights.

syn.note: Easy word; used with 'the': 'the same rights'.
Exactly the same in every detail.
Fair is about right treatment, not exact sameness.

ant.note: Not the same in size, amount or rights.

forms.definition: in the same way or to the same amount
forms.example: The money was shared equally between the three sisters.

syn.note: In parts of the same size.
In a just way; not always the same amount.

ant.note: In a way that is not the same or not fair.

context.text: Our school believes in equality between boys and girls. Every student gets equal time with the teacher, and the prizes are shared equally.

reviewer_note: Inequality and unequal placed as antonyms, not forms. Equation/equate share a Latin root but are not made from equal, so they are left out.

corpus_definition: An imaginary line around the middle of the earth.

forms.definition: an imaginary line around the middle of the earth
forms.example: Countries near the equator are hot all year.
forms.note: Usually 'the equator', sometimes with a capital E.

syn.note: The hot area on both sides of this line, not the line itself.
Latitude measures how far north or south a place is from this line.

forms.note: No verb is made from equator. Equate and equal share an old Latin root but are not made from equator.

forms.definition: near or connected with the imaginary line around the middle of the earth
forms.example: The Amazon has a hot, wet equatorial climate.

syn.note: Tropical covers a wider hot area, not only the middle line.

ant.note: Near the North or South Pole, very far from the middle of the earth.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Uzbekistan is far north of the equator, so our winters can be cold. My cousin lives in Kenya, where the equatorial sun is strong every day.

reviewer_note: Corpus example does not contain the headword; new example written. No affix claimed on equatorial (equatori- is not a word).

corpus_definition: to provide a person or place with necessary tools or supplies

forms.definition: the tools and machines you need for a job or activity
forms.example: The new gym has modern equipment.
forms.note: Uncountable: say 'a piece of equipment', not 'an equipment'.

syn.note: Informal; often for sport or outdoor activities.
Common in British English, especially for sport.
Easy word; tools are things you hold in your hand.
Formal, often for science.

forms.definition: to give a person or place the tools or things they need
forms.example: We must equip the team with the right gear.
forms.note: Pattern: equip someone/something with something. Spelling: equipped, equipping.

syn.note: Provide someone with something: a little more general.
To give things that people need, often regularly.
To fill a room, ship or building with what it needs.
Very easy, general word.

forms.definition: having the tools, skills or things needed for something
forms.example: The hospital is well equipped for emergencies.

syn.note: Ready for something; prepared is more about planning.
Easy word for being able to start.
Only for rooms or homes with furniture.

ant.note: Not having the tools or skills that you need.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Before the hike in the Chimgan mountains, the guide helped us equip ourselves with boots and ropes. All the equipment was checked, so we felt well equipped.

reviewer_note: Equipment is uncountable, noted. Double p in equipped/equipping noted.

corpus_definition: A long period of time in history.

forms.definition: a long period of history with a special character
forms.example: We live in a new era of digital technology.

syn.note: Easy, general word for a length of time.
Used in names: the Stone Age, the digital age.
Formal or scientific; very long or very important.
Very easy, general word: 'in Timur's time'.

forms.note: No verb exists in this family.
No adjective exists in this family.
No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: Samarkand was very rich in the Timurid era. Today a new era of tourism is bringing visitors from all over the world.

reviewer_note: Single-form family; no derived words exist.

corpus_definition: To start a business or organization that will last.

forms.definition: the act of starting a company or organization
forms.example: The establishment of the university took ten years.
forms.note: It can also mean a business or organization itself, for example a hotel or restaurant.

syn.note: The act of starting an organization; a little more formal.
Making something new; wider meaning.
Easy, everyday phrase.

ant.note: When a business or organization stops working for ever.
Formal: officially ending a system or law.

forms.definition: to start a company or organization that will last a long time
forms.example: They hope to establish a new school soon.
forms.note: Another meaning: to find out facts ('establish the cause').

syn.note: Easy phrasal verb with the same meaning.
Usually about schools, cities and companies. Past: founded.
Very easy, general word.
To make something new.

ant.note: To stop a business for ever.
Formal: to officially end a system or law.

forms.definition: having existed for a long time and accepted by people
forms.example: It is an established company with a good name.

syn.note: Having existed for a long time.
Easy word: many people know about it.
Thought to be right or normal by most people.

ant.note: Started only a short time ago.

forms.note: No adverb exists in this family.

context.text: My grandfather helped establish a small bakery in Bukhara in 1985. Today it is an established business, and its establishment is still a proud family story.

reviewer_note: Kept the 'start an organization' sense; 'establish facts' mentioned in a note. Founder is not family, so People & things is empty.
